steps.title: Where to start: work from the inside out
steps.body: Nested parentheses tell you the order: the innermost part must be done first. An exponent of $-1$ means "take the reciprocal", so the whole expression is one move repeated three times: take the reciprocal, then add $1$. Start with $2+1 = 3$.

steps.title: Do the next layer
steps.body:
Now apply the same move to $\frac{4}{3}$. Its reciprocal is $\frac{3}{4}$, and adding $1$ gives $\frac{7}{4}$. Notice a shortcut: taking the reciprocal of $\frac{p}{q}$ and adding $1$ gives $\frac{q}{p}+1 = \frac{p+q}{p}$. So the new numerator is the old numerator plus the old denominator, and the new denominator is the old numerator.
$$\frac{p}{q} \;\longmapsto\; \frac{p+q}{p}$$

your_turn.prompt: Check the shortcut on the first move, from $3 = \frac{3}{1}$ to $\frac{4}{3}$.
your_turn.answer: New numerator $3+1 = 4$, new denominator $3$, so $\frac{4}{3}$. It matches.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Apply the move one last time to $\frac{7}{4}$: the reciprocal is $\frac{4}{7}$, and $\frac{4}{7}+1 = \frac{11}{7}$. Careful: there are three "reciprocal, then add $1$" moves, so do not stop at $\frac{7}{4}$, and do not forget the final $+1$ (which would leave $\frac{4}{7}$). Neither of those is a choice, which is a good warning sign. The answer is **(B)** $\frac{11}{7}$.

verification.verifier_notes: Passed adversarial verifier on first review.
